hint.p: Remember that the derivative of \sec x is \sec x \tan x.
Let u = \sec\mathopen{}\left(-5x\right). Don't forget the chain rule when you find du.
Remember that to integrate something of the form \displaystyle \frac{1}{u^8} you should rewrite as u^{-8} and then use power rule.

solution.p: Let u=\sec\mathopen{}\left(-5x\right). Then we take the derivative of both sides to get du = -5\sec\mathopen{}\left(-5x\right)\tan\mathopen{}\left(-5x\right) \, dx

You can do the next step in different ways, but one way is to solve for dx. Since du = -5\sec\mathopen{}\left(-5x\right)\tan\mathopen{}\left(-5x\right) \, dx, we divide over to get that dx=\frac{1}{-5\sec\mathopen{}\left(-5x\right)\tan\mathopen{}\left(-5x\right)} \, du Then we substitute back into the original integral. \int \frac{8 \sec(-5 x)\tan(-5 x)}{\sec^{8}(-5 x)} \, dx = \int \frac{8 \sec(-5 x)\tan(-5 x)}{u^{8}} \frac{1}{-5\sec\mathopen{}\left(-5x\right)\tan\mathopen{}\left(-5x\right)} \, du Which simplifies to \int -\frac{1.6}{u^{8}}du

Now, this is one of our basic integrals because we can write it as \displaystyle \int -1.6 u^{-8} \, du and thus we can integrate it. Constants in front just stay multiplied so we get \int -1.6 u^{-8} \, du = \frac{-1.6}{-7} u^{-7}+C Finally, make sure you put it back in terms of the original variable, which in this case is 'x'. So we substitute back in for 'u', which was \sec\mathopen{}\left(-5x\right). Thus the final answer to this integral is \int \frac{8 \sec(-5 x)\tan(-5 x)}{\sec^{8}(-5 x)} \, dx = 0.228571\mathopen{}\left(\sec\mathopen{}\left(-5x\right)\right)^{-7}+C
